title: Paying to Punish Free Riders
text:
At the University of Zurich, economists Ernst Fehr and Simon Gachter had students play a public goods game for real money. In groups of four, each player received some money units and secretly decided how many to put into a common project. Whatever went in was multiplied and shared equally among all four. Everyone gained most if all contributed fully, but each individual earned more by keeping their own money and letting others pay.

The groups were reshuffled each round so that players never met the same partners twice. Without any way to respond, cooperation started at a moderate level and steadily fell, as people saw others holding back and cut their own contributions.

In another condition, after seeing what others had contributed, players could pay some of their own money to reduce the earnings of a free rider. Since partners changed every round, punishing could never bring the punisher any future gain. Yet many players did it, often heavily, and they reported anger at free riders. With punishment available, contributions rose and stayed high, and free riding collapsed.
lesson: Cooperation in a group needs a way to respond to people who take without giving. Fair, visible consequences protect those who do their share.
source: Fehr, E., and Gachter, S. (2002). Altruistic punishment in humans. Nature, 415(6868), 137-140.
caveat: Later studies found that in some societies punishment is also aimed at cooperators, which can undermine cooperation instead of supporting it.
